text: Model extraction is a theft attack that never touches your training pipeline, your code, or your weights file. All it needs is the one thing every hosted model has to expose to be useful at all — its prediction API. This lesson is about understanding that risk from a defender's seat, so the next two lessons on real defenses actually make sense.

The pattern is simple. An attacker sends a large number of inputs to a public API, records whatever comes back for each one, and uses those input-output pairs as a labeled training set to train their own substitute model — one that mimics the original's behavior without ever seeing its code or its real training data. Tramer and colleagues' 2016 research showed production-style classifiers reconstructed to near-exact fidelity, sometimes recovering exact parameters, in as few as a couple thousand queries.

How much information an API hands back per query controls how fast that happens. A bare predicted label gives one bit of signal about where the decision boundary sits. A full confidence vector or raw logit score reveals the model's distance from that boundary — exactly the gradient-like signal a substitute model needs to converge fast. Two responses can answer the same business question with wildly different extraction risk: one returns a full confidence vector, the other returns only the label.

This is a real business risk, not an academic curiosity. A model that took months of curated data and compute to build can be approximated in days at a fraction of the cost, wiping out that investment. Many ML products are priced per query precisely because the model is the product — a working substitute model means an attacker never pays for a query again. And once that substitute exists, it becomes a private, unmonitored copy to craft adversarial examples against offline, which frequently transfer back to the real model, a connection you'll dig into in Chapter 5.

None of this requires a sophisticated attacker — it requires an API that answers too precisely, too many times, with nobody watching how it's being used. That's exactly the gap the next two lessons close: rate limiting, anomalous query monitoring, and output minimization, so a model can stay useful to legitimate callers without handing its decision boundary to anyone who queries it enough.
